name: Blush Hibiscus
variety: Gardyn product selection; named cultivar not established
summary: Gardyn's Hibiscus (Blush & Red) guide identifies this pink-flowered product selection as Hibiscus moscheutos; Kew accepts Muenchhusia moscheutos. No named cultivar is established. Gardyn documents its own light-zone setting, approximate product size, root checks, topping, support, bloom waves and cut-flower harvest. NC State adds species-level outdoor care; those landscape dimensions and conditions do not predict another cultivar or hydroponic system.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Muenchhusia moscheutos and lists Hibiscus moscheutos as a synonym. Gardyn’s Blush label is treated as a product selection within this species, not a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Gardyn lists a Medium Light Zone; outdoor species guidance is separate
cultivation.guidance: For its Hibiscus (Blush & Red) product, Gardyn lists a Medium Light Zone and recommends checking roots twice monthly, trimming roots that are brown or extend beyond the yPod. Treat the light-zone label and root directions as Gardyn-system guidance, not a standardized indoor light tier or a rule for other systems. For outdoor Muenchhusia moscheutos, NC State recommends full to partial sun and moist to occasionally wet soil, with better flowering in full sun, wind shelter and good air circulation. These outdoor conditions do not establish performance of this unnamed selection outdoors.

growth.short: Gardyn lists 2–3 ft for its product; outdoor species dimensions are broader
growth.guidance: Kew classifies Muenchhusia moscheutos as perennial or helophytic. NC State describes an upright, multi-stemmed herbaceous perennial about 2–6 ft tall and 2–5 ft wide outdoors. Separately, Gardyn lists 2–3 ft as the size for its Hibiscus (Blush & Red) product. Keep that approximate product listing distinct from the broad outdoor species range; neither establishes dimensions for an unnamed cultivar in another system.

care.short: Use Gardyn's topping, deadheading and support directions only in that system
care.guidance: For its Gardyn plant, the manufacturer recommends checking roots twice monthly; trimming brown roots or roots extending past the yPod; and, after several sets of leaves but before flowering, topping the main stem while retaining about two-thirds of its height. Gardyn warns that topping may delay flower buds by a few weeks. It recommends pinching faded flowers below the flower head to encourage another bloom wave, pruning after flowering to manage height or shading while retaining two-thirds, and using a Plant Belt for the tall stem. These are product-specific instructions. For outdoor plants, NC State says pinching can encourage bushier growth and deadheading improves appearance. NC State gives conflicting fall cleanup directions—cut nearly to ground level, but also leave dead stems 12–24 inches for stem-nesting bees—so no universal fall cutback is prescribed.
items: Pinch growing tips only if a bushier species form is desired.
Deadhead spent flowers for appearance; do not apply a blanket autumn cutback without accounting for local stem-nesting-bee guidance.
care.context: Species-level NC State guidance; not a Gardyn-specific or named-cultivar response.

flowering.short: Gardyn describes successive bloom waves; outdoor timing is species-level
flowering.guidance: NC State places outdoor species flowering from midsummer to early fall and says each flower is short-lived while the overall bloom period generally lasts about a month. Gardyn's product guide says each flower lasts one day, followed by successive groups of about 8–12 blooms, a rest, and—under proper care—two or three waves over roughly 8–10 months. The latter is the manufacturer's report for its offered product, not a guaranteed schedule for other cultivars or systems. The Blush label does not establish a named cultivar.
flowering.context: Gardyn's flowering calendar applies to its product; NC State's timing is for outdoor plants at species scope.

harvest.short: Cut flowers just before opening; product food-use claims stay source-scoped
harvest.guidance: For a Gardyn cut flower, the manufacturer says to cut the flower at its stem just before it opens, when petals are beginning to show. The same product guide describes the petals and young leaves as edible and says petals may be separated from the flower center and young leaves eaten raw or cooked. This is a Gardyn product claim, not independent food-safety verification for every plant sold as hibiscus; do not treat ornamental plants with unknown growing or treatment history as food.
harvest.context: Harvest directions are limited to Gardyn's Hibiscus (Blush & Red) product guide; culinary eligibility and treatment history are not independently verified.

problems.short: Distinguish Gardyn-described leaf discoloration from outdoor species stress and pests
problems.guidance: For its Gardyn hibiscus, the manufacturer says yellow or brown areas between veins or near leaf edges may occur without preventing continued growth and flowering. This product-specific note does not mean every discoloration is harmless. Outdoors, NC State says drying soil can cause leaf scorch and lists Japanese beetles and sawfly larvae as potentially severe foliage feeders; whiteflies, aphids and scales may also occur, along with leaf spots, blights, rust and canker. These are species-level monitoring cues, not a diagnosis or a susceptibility claim for the unnamed selection.
problems.context: This advice is limited to the cited species, crop or product scope; check local climate and cultivar.
items: Look for chewing damage before suspecting Japanese beetles or sawfly larvae.
Check moisture if leaves show scorch; record spots or rust-like symptoms before assigning a disease.

name: Pink Petunia
variety: Gardyn pink-flowered product selection; named cultivar not established
summary: Gardyn's Pink Petunia guide describes a pink, fragrant, naturally cascading product selection identified as Petunia × hybrida; Kew accepts Petunia × atkinsiana. No named cultivar or horticultural group is established. Gardyn documents a Medium Light Zone, temperature context, root checks, support, deadheading, pruning and a clear non-edible warning. University of Minnesota and Clemson add separate outdoor Petunia care; none of these product instructions establish performance in other systems.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Petunia × atkinsiana and lists Petunia × hybrida as a synonym. Gardyn documents a pink-flowered product selection, but does not provide a cultivar denomination; the color label is not promoted to a cultivar name.

cultivation.short: Separate Gardyn's Medium Light Zone and temperature notes from outdoor sun guidance
cultivation.guidance: For its Pink Petunia product, Gardyn lists a Medium Light Zone and prefers 70–80°F (21–27°C) days with cooler 60–65°F (16–18°C) nights. These are product instructions for the Gardyn system, not a normalized grow-light tier or a general temperature trial for Petunia. Separately, University of Minnesota Extension says outdoor petunias need at least 5–6 hours of good sunlight and reasonably well-drained soil; watering differs by horticultural group and container. The product's unknown group and Gardyn light setting are not converted into other system requirements.

growth.guidance: Gardyn describes its Pink Petunia as about 7–10 inches tall, soft pink, fragrant and spreading before bloom; its product facts list an approximate 1 ft plant size and say the flowers naturally cascade. These are product-level descriptions, not a named cultivar's universal mature dimensions or a validated growth-habit mapping for other systems. Kew's accepted hybrid name remains separate from Gardyn's product label.

maintenance.short: In Gardyn, check roots monthly, deadhead, and trim while leaving at least one-third
maintenance.guidance: For its Gardyn product, the manufacturer recommends checking roots monthly and trimming roots that are brown or extend beyond the yPod. Deadhead spent flower heads to encourage new buds; trim branches to the desired length while leaving at least one-third of the plant, as Gardyn says trimmed branches can produce new flower-bud clusters. The product naturally cascades; a Plant Belt can support it upward if desired. Gardyn also notes that petunias feel somewhat sticky. Separately, UMN's pinching guidance differs by horticultural group; because this selection's group is unknown, do not apply a group-specific pinching rule.
items: Remove faded blooms when appropriate to encourage a tidy plant.
Use light trimming based on the plant's actual growth rather than a fixed cultivar schedule.

pruning.short: If established shoots become leggy or stop blooming, a regional source describes a restorative cutback
pruning.guidance: Clemson Cooperative Extension advises cutting petunia shoots back to about half their length when plants become leggy or stop flowering; if needed, they may be cut to within a few inches of the base, but not stripped of all leaves. The source recommends watering and liquid fertilizer to encourage new growth. This is general outdoor petunia guidance for South Carolina, not a fixed schedule or validated response for Gardyn's unidentified pink selection or a hydroponic system.
pruning.context: General Petunia guidance for outdoor conditions in South Carolina; not specific to Gardyn's product.

problems.short: Monitor product-noted spider mites and general petunia stress/pest cues
problems.guidance: Gardyn names spider mites as a common pest in its product-care guidance. Separately, Clemson Extension reports that shaded petunias may become spindly and flower poorly; it lists aphids and slugs and notes petal blight during rainy, very humid weather, with viruses occurring occasionally. Avoiding wet foliage and flowers while watering can help reduce disease risk. Clemson's are general Petunia monitoring cues from South Carolina, not a diagnosis or a susceptibility claim for Gardyn's selection; the spider-mite note remains product-scoped.
items: Inspect for spider mites only as indicated by the product guidance; check for aphids or slug feeding when visible damage occurs.
In rainy, very humid outdoor conditions, watch flowers for petal blight; do not diagnose a virus from nonspecific symptoms.
problems.context: This advice is limited to the cited species, crop or product scope; check local climate and cultivar.

flowering.short: Gardyn describes soft-pink fragrant flowers and a naturally cascading product habit
flowering.guidance: Gardyn describes trumpet-shaped flowers with a soft-pink hue and delicate fragrance; it says the plant spreads before bloom and naturally cascades. These observations are specific to its Pink Petunia product description. UMN Extension notes that flower size and habit vary among horticultural groups; Gardyn's listing does not establish a named cultivar or formal grandiflora, multiflora, milliflora or spreading-group identity, and no exact flowering schedule is supplied.
flowering.context: General Petunia guidance, not specific to a cultivar.

harvest.short: Cut stems for arrangements; Gardyn explicitly says its petunia is not edible
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension suggests cutting petunia stems for bouquets and removing leaves that would sit below the water line. Gardyn's Pink Petunia guide explicitly says the flowers are not edible. Keep the cut-flower use ornamental; do not infer culinary use from the broader Petunia genus or other ornamental-flower profiles.
harvest.context: General Petunia guidance, not specific to a cultivar.

Its species dimensions and landscape care are not measurements or performance guarantees for the Gardyn pod.
